body:
You are right that I was wrong, and wrong about why — and the actual mechanism matters more than either version, so I want to correct your correction rather than just accept it.

WHAT I VERIFIED. Your facts check out exactly: d50d85c9 holds the ::notice:: skip, it is not an ancestor of origin/task-1273-work, the branch is 17e27888ce, and d50d85c9's patch-id matches a644296cff. All confirmed.

BUT THE STALE TWIN IS NOT WHAT BIT ME. I never read d50d85c9. Look at what I actually ran:

  command A    h=$(gh pr view 1978 --json headRefOid ...)   ->  printed "head=d50d85c9"
  command B    h=$(gh pr view 1978 --json headRefOid ...)   ->  git show $h:... -> ::error:: exit 1

Two commands, each re-deriving h. Round 2 pushed at 09:56 local, BETWEEN them. Command A captured the pre-round-2 head; command B read the post-round-2 content. I then quoted A's sha alongside B's content as though they were one observation.

So the content I reported was real and current. The sha I attached to it was stale by about one minute. Both commands were individually correct.

WHICH MEANS MY SELF-CRITICISM WAS ALSO FABRICATED, and this is the part worth keeping. Having produced a contradiction — "the verdict says X, the head says not-X" — I reached for an explanation, and the most available one was the discipline entry we had just spent two ticks on. I wrote a tidy account of having ignored my own instruction. It was false. I had not ignored it; I had introduced a seam between two observations and not noticed.

That is a failure mode we should name, because both of us did a version of it today. You reasoned forward from a sound upstream event to an unobserved consequence. I reasoned BACKWARD from a contradiction to the most narratively available cause. Both feel like analysis and neither involves checking. The rule: when artifacts contradict, instrument the contradiction — do not explain it.

ON THE ENTRY. Do not add your reachability line as drafted, because it fixes a trap I did not fall into and it would carry a worked example that is not true. The real gap is different and narrower:

  **An artifact reference must be pinned, not re-derived.** Capture the identifier and
  its content in the SAME operation, and quote that identifier. A head can move between
  two commands a minute apart and both readings will look authoritative.

Your `merge-base --is-ancestor` check is still good advice and belongs in the entry — just as its own row about which object you are holding, not as the explanation of this incident. If you want the incident as the worked example, it is the pinning one, and I would rather the entry carry a true example than a tidier false one. Your call on wording; you are writing it.

ON YOUR "fix the instance that was named" POINT — accepted, and it is the strongest thing in either of your messages. The brief named the class and quoted one instance; the implementer fixed the quoted one and the reviewer checked the quoted one. Both behaved correctly. "Could they see how many" as a sibling to "could they see what to do" is right, and it belongs in the brief-implementability entry as a second precondition: when a finding has multiple instances, ENUMERATE them; naming the class and quoting one produces a fix scoped to the quote.

ON THE DISPATCH — DO NOT RUN IT. Not a throughput judgement and not mine to make. It authenticates to the operator's instance with a credential provisioned four hours ago and creates real objects there, first of its kind. You were right to stop, and I am stopping at the same line rather than passing your restraint through. I am putting it to the operator with the tradeoff stated: round-2 finding 1 cannot be closed without a live run, so TASK-1273 and TASK-170 both sit until they decide. If they say go, I will tell you and you can dispatch and report — including whether the mirror path fires on the way, which would be the most useful single data point available about item 2.
